claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Iwai et al., 2017

claims.claim: Only a subgroup of patients respond effectively to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
claims.source: Although ICIs showed promising clinical outcomes in cancer patients, often only a subgroup of patients respond effectively (Robert, 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Robert, 2020

claims.claim: Tumor doubling times (around 60–200 days) are orders of magnitude slower than cancer cell doubling times (around 1–2 days).
claims.source: One argument supporting this concept is the observation that tumor doubling times (around 60–200 days) is orders of magnitude slower than cancer cell doubling times (around 1–2 days).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting the concept of NME suppressive function

claims.claim: The majority of cancer cells usually die before they can divide and establish a tumor mass.
claims.source: This argues for a suppressive function of the NME and as a result the majority of cancer cells usually die before they can divide and establish a tumor mass (Klein, 2009; Greaves and Maley, 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Klein, 2009 and Greaves and Maley, 2012

claims.claim: Tumor mutational burden (TMB) is associated with outcomes in patients treated with immunotherapy.
claims.source: One of the key clinical observations in support of the relation between the genomic landscape of lung cancer cells and the TME is the association with tumor mutational burden (TMB), defined as the number of non-synonymous somatic mutations per megabase of tumor DNA, and the outcomes in patients treated with immunotherapy (Litchfield et al., 2021; Snyder et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Litchfield et al., 2021 and Snyder et al., 2014

claims.claim: Recognition of cancer cells by immune cells mainly relies on presentation of tumor-specific antigens by MHC molecules on the surface of cancer cells.
claims.source: Recognition of cancer cells by immune cells mainly relies on presentation of tumor-specific antigens by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules on the surface of cancer cells which prime and activate the immune cells that can ultimately trigger cancer cell death (Schreiber et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Schreiber et al., 2011

claims.claim: TMB can serve as an indicator of neoantigen load of a tumor.
claims.source: Despite the fact that not all somatic mutations will lead to neoantigens, TMB can serves as an indicator of neoantigen load of a tumor (Zou et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Zou et al., 2021

claims.claim: Common lung tumor mutations, including KRAS and TP53, are characterized by a high TMB and numerous somatic mutations, which are associated with increased tumor immunogenicity.
claims.source: In addition, common lung tumor mutations, including KRAS and TP53, are characterized by a high TMB and numerous somatic mutations, which are associated with increased tumor immunogenicity (Dong et al., 2017b; Gao et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2017b and Gao et al., 2020

claims.claim: High TMB correlates with a greater probability of harboring neoantigens and cancer cell driver mutations.
claims.source: Thus, high TMB correlates with a greater probability of harboring neoantigens and cancer cell driver mutations (Chan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 2019

claims.claim: High TMB boosts tumor immunogenicity because more neoantigens are recognized by cytotoxic T cells, which promote the antitumor immune response.
claims.source: High TMB in turn will boost tumor immunogenicity, because more neoantigens are recognized by cytotoxic T cells, which promote the antitumor immune response (Rizvi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Rizvi et al., 2015

claims.claim: In the KEYNOTE-158 study, tumor TMB-high status characterized a subgroup of patients with advanced solid tumors who showed significant tumor remission in response to pembrolizumab.
claims.source: In the KEYNOTE-158 study, tumor TMB-high status characterized a subgroup of patients with advanced solid tumors who showed a significant tumor remission in response to the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody pembrolizumab (Marabelle et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Marabelle et al., 2020

claims.claim: In the CHECKMATE-026 study, high TMB patients treated with nivolumab showed a longer progression-free survival (9.7 vs 5.8 months; HR = 0.62) and higher response rates (47 vs 28%) than patients with the same TMB receiving chemotherapy.
claims.source: High TMB patients treated with the anti PD-1 antibody nivolumab showed a longer progression-free survival (PFS; 9.7 vs 5.8 months; HR  = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.38–1.00) and higher response rates (47 vs 28%) than patients with the same TMB receiving chemotherapy.
claims.evidence: Data from the CHECKMATE-026 study

claims.claim: In the CHECKMATE-026 study, patients with both high TMB and PD-L1 expression in more than 50% of tumor cells had a higher response rate (75%) compared to patients with only one of these factors.
claims.source: Moreover, patients with both high TMB and PD-L1 expression in more than 50% of the tumor cells had a higher response rate (75%) compared to patients with only one of these factors (32% among patients with a high tumor-mutation burden only and 34% among those with a PD-L1 expression level of ≥50% only; Carbone et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Carbone et al., 2016

claims.claim: In the CHECKMATE-227 study, combined treatment with nivolumab plus ipilimumab resulted in a longer PFS compared to chemotherapy (7.2 vs 5.5 months; HR = 0.58) in patients with advanced NSCLC and a TMB status of at least 10 mutations per megabase.
claims.source: In the CHECKMATE-227 study, patients with advanced NSCLC and a TMB status of at least 10 mutations per megabase, the combined treatment with nivolumab plus ipilimumab, an antibody targeting the global negative T cell regulator Cytotoxic T lymphocyte-Associated antigen (CTLA-4), resulted in a longer PFS compared to the chemotherapy group (7.2 vs 5.5 months; HR  = 0.58, 97.5% CI: 0.41–0.81, p < 0.001) (Hellmann et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hellmann et al., 2018

claims.claim: Aneuploidy is positively correlated with the number of mutations in most types of cancer including lung tumor.
claims.source: Aneuploidy has been shown to be positively correlated with the number of mutations in the most types of cancer including lung tumor (Taylor et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2018

claims.claim: Tumor aneuploidy negatively correlates with markers of immune evasion and number of tumor-infiltrating leukocytes.
claims.source: Three groups independently indicated that tumor aneuploidy negatively correlates with markers of immune evasion and number of tumor-infiltrating leukocytes (Davoli et al., 2017; Xian et al., 2021; Taylor et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Davoli et al., 2017, Xian et al., 2021, and Taylor et al., 2018

claims.claim: Highly aneuploid tumors show significantly reduced expression of genes associated with adaptive immunity, high cytotoxic activity mediated by CD8+ T cells and pathways related to pro-inflammatory cytokines.
claims.source: Davoli et al. reported a significantly reduced expression of genes associated with adaptive immunity, high cytotoxic activity mediated by CD8+ T cells and pathways related to the presence of pro-inflammatory cytokines in high aneuploid tumors.
claims.evidence: Findings from Davoli et al. study

claims.claim: Highly aneuploid tumors are associated with poorer survival of patients.
claims.source: Moreover, they found highly aneuploid tumors to be associated with poorer survival of patients (Davoli et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Davoli et al., 2017

claims.claim: KRAS mutations are the most frequent oncogenic driver mutations in human lung cancer cells.
claims.source: KRAS mutations are the most frequent oncogenic driver mutations in human lung cancer cells (Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014; Jordan et al., 2017; Skoulidis et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Cancer Genome Atlas Research, 2014, Jordan et al., 2017, and Skoulidis et al., 2015

claims.claim: In lung cancer positive for oncogenic KRAS mutations, a pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressed TME enriched in pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs, IL-17-producing Th17 cells and CD4+FoxP3+ Treg cells has been found.
claims.source: Specifically, in lung cancer positive for oncogenic KRAS mutations, a pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressed TME enriched in pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs, interleukin (IL)–17-producing T helper (Th)17 cells and CD4+FoxP3+ Treg cells has been found (Cullis et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Cullis et al., 2018 and depicted in Figure 2A

claims.claim: KRAS is a small GTPase and an activator of MAPK pathways.
claims.source: KRAS is a small GTPase and an activator of MAPK pathways (Joneson et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Joneson et al., 1996

claims.claim: Mutant RAS proteins activate the NF-κB pathway in cancer cells.
claims.source: It has also long been known that mutant RAS proteins activate the nuclear factor of kappa light polypeptide gene enhancer of the B-cells (NF-κB) pathway in cancer cells (Cullis et al., 2018; Finco et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Cullis et al., 2018, Finco et al., 1997, and Kim et al., 2002

claims.claim: NF-κB-binding sites are found in the enhancers and promoters of numerous immunoregulatory genes.
claims.source: As NF-κB-binding sites are found in the enhancers and promoters of numerous immunoregulatory genes (Natoli et al., 2005), it is not surprising that NF-κB plays a pivotal role in cancer by fueling a pro-tumorigenic inflammatory environment through the induction of classical NF-κB target genes (Baud and Karin, 2009; DiDonato et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Natoli et al., 2005, Baud and Karin, 2009, and DiDonato et al., 2012

claims.claim: NF-κB target genes comprise cytokines and chemokines including IL6, TNFα, IL-1α/β, CXCL1, 2, 5, and 8, CCL2, and ICAM1 as well as regulatory cell cycle and anti-apoptotic proteins.
claims.source: These genes comprise a plethora of cytokines and chemokines, including IL6, tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα), IL-1α/β, CXCL1, 2, 5, and 8, monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) / CCL2, and intracellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1) as well as regulatory cell cycle and anti-apoptotic proteins (Baud and Karin, 2009; Eluard et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Baud and Karin, 2009 and Eluard et al., 2020

claims.claim: By secreting IL-6, mutant KRAS cancer cells can activate JAK1 to induce the phosphorylation of STAT3 in immune components such as macrophages of the TME.
claims.source: By secreting IL-6, mutant KRAS cancer cells can activate Janus activated kinase 1 (JAK1) to induce the phosphorylation of the transcription factor signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) which is found in immune components such as macrophages of the TME (reviewed in Chonov et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chonov et al., 2019

claims.claim: Pharmacological blockade of IL-6 suppresses progression of KRAS-mutant positive lung cancer, inhibits STAT3 activation and diminishes the number of pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs and Treg cells while CD8+ T-cell responses increase.
claims.source: Studies in preclinical mouse models showed that the pharmacological blockade of IL-6 suppresses progression of KRAS-mutant positive lung cancer, inhibits STAT3 activation and more importantly diminishes the number of pro-tumor M2 macrophages, MDSCs and Treg cells while the CD8+ T-cell responses increases (Caetano et al., 2016, Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Caetano et al., 2016 and depicted in Figure 2A

claims.claim: Mutant KRASG12V transcriptionally induces CXCL8 through the RAF-MAPK, PI3K and NF-κB signaling pathways.
claims.source: Seminal work by Bar-Sagi et al. showed that mutant KRASG12V transcriptionally induces CXCL8 through the RAF-MAPK, PI3K and NF-κB signaling pathways (Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004

claims.claim: A neutralizing anti-CXCL8 antibody attenuates survival and neo-angiogenesis in a non-cell-autonomous manner and reduces the infiltration of inflammatory immune cells in a mouse xenograft tumor model.
claims.source: Using a mouse xenograft tumor model, a neutralizing anti-CXCL8 antibody was shown to attenuate survival and neo-angiogenesis in a non-cell-autonomous manner and to reduce the infiltration of inflammatory immune cells (Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Sparmann and Bar-Sagi, 2004

claims.claim: Lung tissues derived from the KrasG12D LA1 lung adenocarcinoma mouse model showed higher concentrations of the CXCL8 functional homologues KC and MIP-2.
claims.source: Likewise, the lung tissues derived from the KrasG12D LA1 lung adenocarcinoma mouse model showed higher concentrations of the CXCL8 functional homologues KC and MIP-2 (Wislez et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wislez et al., 2006

claims.claim: Antibody-based blockade of the CXCR2 receptor reduces the frequency and progression of lung tumors.
claims.source: The reduced frequency and progression of lung tumors following antibody-based blockade of the CXCR2 receptor is further evidence for the role CXCL8 plays in tumorigenesis (Wislez et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wislez et al., 2006

claims.claim: IL-1α or IL-1β can induce the transcriptional and post-transcriptional expression of IL-6, CXCL8 and multiple other chemokines simultaneously through a network of signaling pathways and transcription factors in multiple normal as well as cancer cells.
claims.source: IL-6, CXCL8 and multiple other chemokines (e.g. CXCL1, 2, 3, 5, CCL20, CCL2) are under complex control of 'master cytokines' such as IL-1α or IL-1β, which can induce the transcriptional and post-transcriptional expression of all of these factors simultaneously through a network of signaling pathways and transcription factors (including the NF-κB system) in multiple normal as well as cancer cells from both mice or humans (Gaestel et al., 2009; Jurida et al., 2015; Weber et al., 2010; Wolter et al., 2008; Ziesché et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Gaestel et al., 2009, Jurida et al., 2015, Weber et al., 2010, Wolter et al., 2008, and Ziesché et al., 2013

claims.claim: The IL-1 system can be pharmacologically targeted by IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), the anti IL-1β antibody canakinumab, or a recombinant IL-1 receptor IgG fusion protein called rilonacept.
claims.source: The IL-1 system can be successfully pharmacologically targeted in a range of chronic inflammatory conditions by the (i) IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), (ii) the fully human anti IL-1β antibody canakinumab, or (iii) a recombinant IL-1 receptor IgG fusion protein called rilonacept (Dinarello et al., 2012; Mantovani et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Dinarello et al., 2012 and Mantovani et al., 2019a

claims.claim: IL-1RA is equally effective in suppressing IL-1α and IL-1β, while canakinumab is IL-1β-specific.
claims.source: Of note, the IL-1RA is equally effective in suppressing IL-1α and IL-1β, while canakinumab is IL-1β-specific (Dinarello et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dinarello et al., 2012

claims.claim: Nuclear IL-1α acts as a signal for genotoxic stress and binds to sites of DNA damage and thereby regulates tissue inflammation.
claims.source: They showed that nuclear IL-1α acts as a signal for genotoxic stress and binds to sites of DNA damage and thereby regulates tissue inflammation (Cohen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2015

claims.claim: Lack of IL-1β or excess of IL-1 activity in the lung TME both resulted in reduced T cell activity and a poor prognosis.
claims.source: Using IL-1β or IL-1RA-deficient mice, they found that lack of IL-1β or excess of IL-1 activity (by lack of IL-1RA) in the lung TME both resulted in reduced T cell activity and a poor prognosis.
claims.evidence: Findings from experimental studies with knockout mice

claims.claim: IL-1β-deficient mice showed increased Treg numbers and activities whereas in IL-1RA-deficient mice enhanced accumulation and activity of myeloid-derived suppressor cells were found, both resulting in suppressed antitumor immunity.
claims.source: IL-1β-deficient mice showed increased Treg numbers and activities whereas in IL-1RA-deficient mice enhanced accumulation and activity of myeloid-derived suppressor cells were found, both resulting in suppressed antitumor immunity.
claims.evidence: Findings from experimental studies with knockout mice

claims.claim: In mice lacking IL-17, reduced tumor progression along with improved T cell function was observed.
claims.source: In mice lacking IL-17, the study showed reduced tumor progression along with improved T cell function.
claims.evidence: Findings from experimental studies with knockout mice

claims.claim: KRAS mutations in lung epithelial cells lead to the recruitment of Th17 cells and increased IL-17 production, both of which are associated with lung tumorigenesis.
claims.source: Further studies corroborate the importance of the IL-1/IL-17 axis also for KRAS-driven lung cancer. KRAS mutations in lung epithelial cells lead to the recruitment of Th17 cells and increased IL-17 production, both of which are associated with lung tumorigenesis (Chang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2014

claims.claim: IL-17 secreted from tumor-infiltrating Th17 lymphocytes can induce the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) gene-regulatory events in lung cancer cells, thereby promoting tumor cell migration, intravasation, and metastasis.
claims.source: IL-17 secreted from tumor-infiltrating Th17 lymphocytes can induce the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) gene-regulatory events in lung cancer cells, thereby promoting tumor cell migration, intravasation, and metastasis (Salazar et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Salazar et al., 2020

claims.claim: The blockade of IL-17 in mouse cancer models results in a reduction of lung tumor metastasis.
claims.source: Accordingly and in line with the results from Apte et al., the blockade of IL-17 in mouse cancer models results in a reduction of lung tumor metastasis and the genetic ablation of IL-17C in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model improved the response to anti-PD1 treatment (Ritzmann et al., 2019), (Chang et al., 2014; Salazar et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ritzmann et al., 2019, Chang et al., 2014, and Salazar et al., 2020, and depicted in Figure 2A

claims.claim: The genetic ablation of IL-17C in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model improved the response to anti-PD1 treatment.
claims.source: Accordingly and in line with the results from Apte et al., the blockade of IL-17 in mouse cancer models results in a reduction of lung tumor metastasis and the genetic ablation of IL-17C in a KrasG12D lung cancer mouse model improved the response to anti-PD1 treatment (Ritzmann et al., 2019), (Chang et al., 2014; Salazar et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ritzmann et al., 2019, Chang et al., 2014, and Salazar et al., 2020, and depicted in Figure 2A

claims.claim: The numbers of Th17 lymphocytes in patients with lung cancer negatively correlate with overall survival.
claims.source: Moreover, the numbers of Th17 lymphocytes in patients with lung cancer negatively correlate with overall survival (Salazar et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Salazar et al., 2020

claims.claim: IL-1α is mainly immunostimulatory while IL-1β that is secreted into the TME is mainly pro-inflammatory and promotes tumorigenesis, tumor invasiveness, and immunosuppression.
claims.source: Based on their own results and observations from other studies, Apte et al. concluded that IL-1α and IL-1β play opposing roles in the malignant process. While the membrane-associated IL-1α is mainly immunostimulatory, IL-1β that is secreted into the TME is mainly pro-inflammatory and promotes tumorigenesis, tumor invasiveness, and immunosuppression.
claims.evidence: Conclusion from Apte et al. based on their studies

claims.claim: In a murine breast cancer model, IL-1β-deficiency resulted in IL-12 secretion by CD11b+ dendritic cells and supported antitumor immunity by activated CD8+ lymphocytes expressing IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B.
claims.source: In a murine breast cancer model, IL-1β-deficiency resulted in IL-12 secretion by CD11b+ dendritic cells (DCs) cells and supported antitumor immunity by activated CD8+ lymphocytes expressing IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B.
claims.evidence: Findings from a murine breast cancer model study

claims.claim: Treating mice first with anti-IL-1β antibodies followed by anti-PD-1 antibodies completely abrogated tumor progression.
claims.source: Treating mice first with anti-IL-1β antibodies followed by anti-PD-1 antibodies completely abrogated tumor progression. These data define microenvironmental IL-1β as a master cytokine in tumor progression whose suppression also facilitates successful therapeutic checkpoint inhibition (Kaplanov et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kaplanov et al., 2019

claims.claim: In the CANTOS trial, treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer incidence (HR = 0.33 for the canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo).
claims.source: Unexpectedly, the prespecified safety analysis of the trial data also revealed that treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer incidence (HR = 0.33; 95% CI, 0.18–0.59; p<0.0001 for the canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) as well as lung cancer mortality (HR = 0.23; 95% CI, 0.10–0.54; p<0.0002 for canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) (Crossman and Rothman, 2018; Ridker et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Crossman and Rothman, 2018 and Ridker et al., 2017b

claims.claim: In the CANTOS trial, treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer mortality (HR = 0.23 for canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo).
claims.source: Unexpectedly, the prespecified safety analysis of the trial data also revealed that treatment with canakinumab was associated with a dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer incidence (HR = 0.33; 95% CI, 0.18–0.59; p<0.0001 for the canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) as well as lung cancer mortality (HR = 0.23; 95% CI, 0.10–0.54; p<0.0002 for canakinumab 300 mg group compared with placebo) (Crossman and Rothman, 2018; Ridker et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Crossman and Rothman, 2018 and Ridker et al., 2017b

claims.claim: COSMIC database ctDNA mutations were detected in 65% (46/71) of the CANTOS patients with lung cancer.
claims.source: Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) database ctDNA mutations were detected in 65% (46/71) of the CANTOS patients with lung cancer but none of the mutations commonly found in lung cancer were enriched (or depleted) following canakinumab treatment.
claims.evidence: Data from CANTOS follow-up study

claims.claim: Median time to lung cancer diagnosis was shorter in CANTOS patients with detectable COSMIC ctDNA mutations at baseline (407 days) versus without (837 days).
claims.source: Further, median time to lung cancer diagnosis was shorter in patients with (n=29, 407 days) versus without (n=38, 837 days) detectable COSMIC ctDNA mutations at baseline (p=0.011).
claims.evidence: Data from CANTOS follow-up study

claims.claim: High baseline levels of CRP and IL-6 trended toward shorter median time to lung cancer diagnosis.
claims.source: High baseline levels of CRP and IL-6 trended toward shorter median time to lung cancer diagnosis, suggesting that IL-1β-inducible CRP and IL-6, similar to ctDNA at baseline, correlate positively with a more rapid progression to lung cancer diagnosis (Wong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2020

claims.claim: EGFR mutations in lung cancer cells can upregulate the intrinsic PD-L1 expression on cancer cells, suppress T cell function and increase levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines within the TME.
claims.source: The clinical outcomes of immune checkpoint therapies have revealed that EGFR mutations in lung cancer cells can not only upregulate the intrinsic PD-L1 expression on cancer cells but also suppress T cell function and increase levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines within the TME, which marks an immune escape phenotype of EGFR-mutant NSCLC (Akbay et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Akbay et al., 2013 and Chen et al., 2015

claims.claim: Patients with EGFR mutations have fewer T cell infiltrations of PD-L1+/CD8+ tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and reduced shrinking properties of the tumor in response to immune cell activation.
claims.source: Moreover, it has been shown that patients with EGFR mutations have fewer T cell infiltrations of PD-L1+/CD8+ tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and reduced shrinking properties of the tumor in response to immune cell activation (Figure 2C, Dong et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 2017a and depicted in Figure 2C

claims.claim: Patients with oncogenic EML4-ALK rearrangements showed a significant increase in regulatory T cells compared to the reduced number of cytotoxic T cells in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas.
claims.source: In comparison to the reduced number of cytotoxic T cells in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas, patients with oncogenic EML4-ALK rearrangements showed a significant increase in regulatory T cells, supporting the concept that different driver oncogenes induce distinct immunosuppressive mechanisms (Budczies et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Budczies et al., 2022

claims.claim: MYC activation is involved in the regulation of cell-cycle progression, apoptosis, cellular senescence, and metabolism.
claims.source: MYC activation is involved in the regulation of cell-cycle progression, apoptosis, cellular senescence, and metabolism (Gabay et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gabay et al., 2014

claims.claim: Co-occurrence of MYC genetic alterations with KRAS mutations considerably accelerates lung tumor development with a reduction of the survival rate in mouse lung tumor models.
claims.source: Co-occurrence of MYC genetic alterations with KRAS mutations considerably accelerates lung tumor development with a reduction of the survival rate in mouse lung tumor models (Kortlever et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kortlever et al., 2017

claims.claim: MYC-induced immunosuppression relies on CCL9 and IL-23.
claims.source: Mechanistically, MYC-induced immunosuppression relies on CCL9 and IL-23.
claims.evidence: Mechanistic finding from studies on MYC

claims.claim: CCL9 regulates the recruitment of CD206+ pro-tumor macrophages and PD-L1-dependent expulsion of T and B cells.
claims.source: CCL9 regulates the recruitment of CD206+ pro-tumor macrophages and PD-L1-dependent expulsion of T and B cells.
claims.evidence: Mechanistic finding about CCL9 function

claims.claim: IL-23 boosts the pro-tumor CCL9 effects through the elimination of adaptive T and B cells and innate immune NK cells.
claims.source: IL-23 boosts the pro-tumor CCL9 effects through the elimination of adaptive T and B cells and innate immune NK cells (Kortlever et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kortlever et al., 2017

claims.claim: Blocking of CCL9 and IL-23 abrogates the lung tumor aggressiveness in KRAS/MYC-altered mice mainly by re-establishing a tumor-suppressive lung microenvironment.
claims.source: Blocking of CCL9 and IL-23 abrogates the lung tumor aggressiveness in KRAS/MYC-altered mice mainly by re-establishing a tumor-suppressive lung microenvironment (Kortlever et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kortlever et al., 2017

claims.claim: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in cancer and across all types of lung cancer with mutations rates ranging from 46% in lung adenocarcinoma to over 90% in SCLC.
claims.source: TP53, encoding the tumor suppressive transcription factor p53, is not only the most frequently mutated genes in cancer but also across all types of lung cancer with mutations rates ranging from 46% in lung adenocarcinoma to over 90% in SCLC (Gibbons et al., 2014; George et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Gibbons et al., 2014 and George et al., 2015

claims.claim: TP53-mutant tumors show a distinct TME profile including increased PD-L1 expression and CD8+ T cell infiltration, which suggest an adaptive immune resistance and a high immunogenicity state.
claims.source: TP53-mutant tumors show a distinct TME profile including increased PD-L1 expression and CD8+ T cell infiltration, which suggest an adaptive immune resistance and a high immunogenicity state (Dong et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 2017b and depicted in Figure 2B

claims.claim: Excess of TP53 mutations in lung cancer cells can elevate NF-κB activity.
claims.source: The excess of TP53 mutations in lung cancer cells can also elevate NF-κB activity (Scian et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Scian et al., 2005

claims.claim: Enhanced activation of NF-κB suppresses p53-mediated gene activation and thereby promotes resistance to apoptosis in cancer cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, enhanced activation of NF-κB suppresses p53-mediated gene activation and thereby promotes resistance to apoptosis in cancer cells (Webster and Perkins, 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Webster and Perkins, 1999

claims.claim: In KRAS-mutant lung cancer cells with TP53 co-mutations, increased NF-κB signaling conferred pro-survival signals to the cancer cells.
claims.source: In KRAS-mutant lung cancer cells with TP53 co-mutations, increased NF-κB signaling conferred pro-survival signals to the cancer cells (Meylan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Meylan et al., 2009

claims.claim: KRAS/TP53 lung tumors are characterized by increased expression of PD-L1 and a higher proportion of PD-L1+/CD8a+ T cells compared to KRAS or TP53 single mutation.
claims.source: With regard to TME phenotype, KRAS/TP53 lung tumors are further characterized by increased expression of PD-L1 and a higher proportion of PD-L1+/CD8a+ T cells compared to KRAS or TP53 single mutation (Dong et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 2017b and depicted in Figure 2B

claims.claim: TP53 inactivation in lung adenocarcinomas activates PAQR11-mediated prometastatic secretory vesicle biogenesis in the Golgi, resulting in the autocrine activation of a PLAU receptor/STAT3/PAQR11 feedforward signaling loop that triggers an immunosuppressive TME rich in effector/memory CD8+ T cells and M1 macrophages.
claims.source: For example, TP53 inactivation in lung adenocarcinomas was found to activate progestin and adipoQ receptor 11 (PAQR11)-mediated prometastatic secretory vesicle biogenesis in the Golgi, resulting in the autocrine activation of a PLAU receptor/STAT3/PAQR11 feedforward signaling loop that triggers an immunosuppressive TME rich in effector/memory CD8+ T cells and M1 macrophages (Tan et al., 2021a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tan et al., 2021a

claims.claim: TP53 loss induces G55-dependent secretion that promotes angiogenesis and CD8+ T cell exhaustion.
claims.source: Similarly, TP53 loss induces Golgi reassembly and stacking protein 55 kD (G55)-dependent secretion that promotes angiogenesis and CD8+ T cell exhaustion (Tan et al., 2021b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Tan et al., 2021b

results.result: Lung cancer epidemiology and clinical context: Lung cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer with highest mortality burden worldwide. NSCLC comprises 85% and SCLC 15% of cases. Five-year survival drops from 56% to 6% with metastasis, the lowest among common cancers. Recent decades show mortality decline attributed to reduced smoking, early diagnosis, and new therapies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are all supported by appropriate citations to epidemiological studies and reviews. These are well-established facts in the lung cancer field that provide necessary background context. The statistics cited are consistent with current cancer registry data.

results.result: Lung cancer mutational landscape: Lung cancers are among the most highly mutated tumors, with KRAS, EGFR, ALK, TP53, and LKB1 as the most commonly mutated genes. KRAS mutations are the most frequent oncogenic driver mutations in human lung cancer cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C10, and C33 are supported by citations to large-scale genomic studies including TCGA. These findings are well-established in the literature and represent consensus knowledge about lung cancer genomics.

results.result: Tumor microenvironment composition and function: Non-transformed cells in tumors have pivotal roles in tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis. The TME is a double-edged sword with anti-tumor activities early but may promote progression later. TME contains pro-tumorigenic cells (M2-macrophages, MDSCs, Treg cells) and anti-tumorigenic cells (M1-macrophages, CD8+ T cells, NK cells). Immune checkpoint inhibitors disrupt PD-L1/PD-1 interactions, but only a subgroup of patients respond effectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16 are well-supported by appropriate citations to established TME biology literature. These represent consensus understanding of TME composition and immune checkpoint biology. The limitation of ICI response is a well-documented clinical observation.

results.result: Tumor growth kinetics suggest microenvironment suppression: Tumor doubling times (60-200 days) are orders of magnitude slower than cancer cell doubling times (1-2 days), arguing for suppressive function of the normal microenvironment where the majority of cancer cells die before establishing a tumor mass.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 present a logical inference supported by citations. The discrepancy between cell and tumor doubling times is well-documented and the interpretation that this reflects microenvironmental suppression is reasonable, though alternative explanations (nutrient limitation, spatial constraints) could also contribute.

results.result: Tumor mutational burden and immunogenicity: TMB (non-synonymous mutations per megabase) is associated with immunotherapy outcomes. Cancer cell recognition relies on MHC presentation of tumor antigens. TMB serves as an indicator of neoantigen load. Common lung mutations (KRAS, TP53) have high TMB associated with increased immunogenicity. High TMB correlates with greater neoantigen probability and boosts immunogenicity through cytotoxic T cell recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by appropriate citations establishing the TMB-immunotherapy response relationship. The mechanistic connection through neoantigen presentation is well-established. However, the relationship is correlative rather than definitively causal, and TMB is an imperfect predictor of response.

results.result: Clinical trial evidence for TMB as predictive biomarker: In KEYNOTE-158, TMB-high status predicted tumor remission with pembrolizumab. In CHECKMATE-026, high TMB patients on nivolumab showed longer PFS (9.7 vs 5.8 months, HR=0.62) and higher response rates (47% vs 28%) than chemotherapy. Combined high TMB and PD-L1 >50% showed 75% response rate. In CHECKMATE-227, nivolumab plus ipilimumab resulted in longer PFS (7.2 vs 5.5 months, HR=0.58) in TMB ≥10 mut/Mb patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 report specific clinical trial results with appropriate citations. The data are from published trials with statistical measures provided. These represent important evidence for TMB as a predictive biomarker, though the authors appropriately note in the discussion that TMB has limitations and standardization issues.

results.result: Aneuploidy correlates with immune phenotype: Aneuploidy is positively correlated with mutation number in most cancers including lung. Tumor aneuploidy negatively correlates with immune evasion markers and tumor-infiltrating leukocytes. Highly aneuploid tumors show reduced expression of adaptive immunity genes, CD8+ T cell cytotoxic activity, and pro-inflammatory cytokine pathways, and are associated with poorer patient survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by citations to three independent studies showing consistent findings. The negative correlation between aneuploidy and immune infiltration is well-documented. However, the mechanistic basis for this relationship remains incompletely understood and may involve multiple pathways.

results.result: KRAS mutations create immunosuppressive TME through NF-κB: KRAS-mutant lung cancers show pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressed TME enriched in M2 macrophages, MDSCs, Th17 cells, and Treg cells. KRAS is a GTPase activating MAPK pathways. Mutant RAS activates NF-κB pathway in cancer cells. NF-κB binding sites are in enhancers/promoters of immunoregulatory genes. NF-κB target genes include cytokines/chemokines (IL6, TNFα, IL-1α/β, CXCL1/2/5/8, CCL2, ICAM1) and cell cycle/anti-apoptotic proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are well-supported by citations establishing the KRAS-NF-κB-cytokine axis. The connection between KRAS mutation and immunosuppressive TME is documented, and the NF-κB pathway's role in cytokine production is well-established. This represents a mechanistic framework linking oncogenic mutation to TME phenotype.

results.result: IL-6/JAK1/STAT3 axis in KRAS-mutant tumors: Mutant KRAS cancer cells secrete IL-6, activating JAK1 to induce STAT3 phosphorylation in TME macrophages. Pharmacological IL-6 blockade in preclinical mouse models suppresses KRAS-mutant lung cancer progression, inhibits STAT3 activation, and diminishes M2 macrophages, MDSCs, and Treg cells while increasing CD8+ T-cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by appropriate citations. The IL-6/STAT3 pathway is well-characterized in cancer biology. The preclinical evidence from mouse models is compelling, though translation to human patients requires clinical validation. The mechanistic connection is biologically plausible.

results.result: CXCL8 role in KRAS-driven tumorigenesis: Mutant KRASG12V transcriptionally induces CXCL8 through RAF-MAPK, PI3K, and NF-κB pathways. Anti-CXCL8 antibody attenuates survival and neo-angiogenesis and reduces inflammatory immune cell infiltration in mouse xenografts. KrasG12D mouse model shows elevated CXCL8 homologues (KC, MIP-2). CXCR2 receptor blockade reduces lung tumor frequency and progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by citations to mechanistic studies and mouse models. The CXCL8 pathway's role in KRAS-driven tumorigenesis is well-documented across multiple experimental systems. The convergent evidence from different approaches strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: IL-1 as master cytokine regulating chemokine networks: IL-1α/β can induce transcriptional and post-transcriptional expression of IL-6, CXCL8, and multiple chemokines simultaneously through signaling pathway networks including NF-κB in normal and cancer cells. The IL-1 system can be pharmacologically targeted by IL-1RA, canakinumab (anti-IL-1β antibody), or rilonacept (IL-1 receptor IgG fusion). IL-1RA suppresses both IL-1α and IL-1β, while canakinumab is IL-1β-specific.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are well-supported by citations to IL-1 biology literature. The concept of IL-1 as a master regulator of cytokine networks is well-established. The pharmacological agents mentioned are clinically approved drugs with well-characterized mechanisms of action.

results.result: IL-1α and IL-1β have distinct roles in lung TME: Nuclear IL-1α acts as a genotoxic stress signal binding DNA damage sites, regulating tissue inflammation. In mouse models, both IL-1β deficiency and excess IL-1 activity (IL-1RA deficiency) resulted in reduced T cell activity and poor prognosis. IL-1β-deficient mice showed increased Treg numbers/activities; IL-1RA-deficient mice showed enhanced MDSC accumulation/activity, both suppressing antitumor immunity. IL-17-deficient mice showed reduced tumor progression with improved T cell function.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by citations to studies using knockout mouse models. The findings reveal complex, non-linear relationships where both deficiency and excess of IL-1 activity can be detrimental. This highlights the importance of balance in immune regulation, though the specific mechanisms in human tumors may differ.

results.result: IL-1/IL-17 axis in KRAS-driven lung cancer: KRAS mutations in lung epithelial cells lead to Th17 cell recruitment and increased IL-17 production, associated with tumorigenesis. IL-17 from tumor-infiltrating Th17 cells induces EMT in lung cancer cells, promoting migration, intravasation, and metastasis. IL-17 blockade in mouse models reduces lung tumor metastasis. IL-17C genetic ablation in KrasG12D mice improved anti-PD1 response. Th17 lymphocyte numbers in lung cancer patients negatively correlate with overall survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by citations to multiple studies showing consistent findings across mouse models and human correlative data. The IL-17 pathway's role in KRAS-driven lung cancer is well-documented. The connection to immunotherapy response adds clinical relevance.

results.result: Opposing roles of IL-1α and IL-1β in malignancy: Based on multiple studies, Apte et al. concluded that membrane-associated IL-1α is mainly immunostimulatory while secreted IL-1β is mainly pro-inflammatory, promoting tumorigenesis, invasiveness, and immunosuppression. In murine breast cancer, IL-1β-deficiency resulted in IL-12 secretion by CD11b+ dendritic cells and antitumor immunity by activated CD8+ lymphocytes expressing IFNγ, TNFα, and granzyme B. Sequential treatment with anti-IL-1β then anti-PD-1 antibodies completely abrogated tumor progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by citations to studies from the Apte laboratory and others. The distinction between IL-1α and IL-1β functions is supported by experimental evidence, though the generalizability across different tumor types requires further validation. The combination therapy result is compelling but from a single study.

results.result: CANTOS trial: IL-1β blockade reduces lung cancer incidence and mortality: In the CANTOS trial, canakinumab treatment showed dose-dependent reduction in lung cancer incidence (HR=0.33 for 300mg vs placebo) and mortality (HR=0.23 for 300mg vs placebo). COSMIC ctDNA mutations were detected in 65% of lung cancer patients. Median time to diagnosis was shorter with detectable baseline ctDNA mutations (407 vs 837 days). High baseline CRP and IL-6 trended toward shorter time to diagnosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 report findings from the CANTOS trial with appropriate citations. The lung cancer findings were unexpected secondary outcomes from a cardiovascular trial, which raises questions about mechanism and generalizability. The ctDNA analysis provides additional mechanistic insight. However, these were post-hoc analyses requiring prospective validation.

results.result: EGFR mutations create distinct immunosuppressive TME: EGFR mutations upregulate intrinsic PD-L1 expression on cancer cells, suppress T cell function, and increase pro-inflammatory cytokines in the TME, marking an immune escape phenotype. EGFR-mutant patients have fewer PD-L1+/CD8+ TIL infiltrations and reduced tumor shrinking in response to immune activation. EML4-ALK rearrangements show increased regulatory T cells compared to reduced cytotoxic T cells in EGFR-mutant tumors, supporting that different driver oncogenes induce distinct immunosuppressive mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by appropriate citations. The distinct TME phenotypes associated with different driver mutations are well-documented. The comparison between EGFR and ALK alterations highlights mutation-specific immune effects. This explains differential ICI responses across molecular subtypes.

results.result: MYC/KRAS cooperation creates immunosuppressive TME: MYC regulates cell-cycle progression, apoptosis, senescence, and metabolism. MYC/KRAS co-occurrence accelerates lung tumor development and reduces survival in mouse models. MYC-induced immunosuppression relies on CCL9 and IL-23. CCL9 recruits CD206+ pro-tumor macrophages and causes PD-L1-dependent T/B cell expulsion. IL-23 boosts CCL9 effects by eliminating adaptive T/B cells and innate NK cells. Blocking CCL9 and IL-23 abrogates tumor aggressiveness in KRAS/MYC mice by re-establishing tumor-suppressive microenvironment.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C73 are supported by citations to mouse model studies. The mechanistic pathway from MYC/KRAS through CCL9/IL-23 to immune suppression is well-characterized in the cited work. The therapeutic intervention data strengthen the causal interpretation, though translation to human tumors requires validation.

results.result: TP53 mutations shape inflamed immunosuppressive TME: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in cancer, with 46% in lung adenocarcinoma to >90% in SCLC. TP53-mutant tumors show increased PD-L1 expression and CD8+ T cell infiltration, suggesting adaptive immune resistance and high immunogenicity. TP53 mutations elevate NF-κB activity. Enhanced NF-κB suppresses p53-mediated gene activation, promoting apoptosis resistance. In KRAS/TP53 co-mutant cells, increased NF-κB confers pro-survival signals. KRAS/TP53 tumors show increased PD-L1 expression and higher PD-L1+/CD8a+ T cells compared to single mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 are supported by appropriate citations. The high frequency of TP53 mutations and their association with distinct TME phenotypes are well-documented. The NF-κB connection provides mechanistic insight. The co-mutation analysis reveals synergistic effects on TME phenotype.

results.result: TP53 mutations affect protein secretion machinery: TP53 inactivation activates PAQR11-mediated prometastatic secretory vesicle biogenesis, resulting in PLAU receptor/STAT3/PAQR11 feedforward loop triggering immunosuppressive TME. TP53 loss induces G55-dependent secretion promoting angiogenesis and CD8+ T cell exhaustion. Missense TP53 mutations induce endoplasmic reticulum UDPase ENTPD5 driving the calnexin/calreticulin cycle for secreted protein folding.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by citations to recent mechanistic studies. These findings reveal non-canonical functions of TP53 in regulating secretory pathways. The evidence is compelling but represents relatively recent discoveries that may require additional validation across different contexts.

results.result: KRAS/LKB1 co-mutations alter serine metabolism affecting T cells: KRAS/LKB1 co-mutation occurs in ~25% of KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinomas. LKB1 is a serine-threonine kinase regulating metabolism and energy stress through AMPK. KRAS/LKB1 cooperation induces the serine-glycine-one-carbon pathway, enhancing SAM synthesis for DNA methylation. Extracellular serine is essential for T cell expansion through glycine and one-carbon units for nucleotide biosynthesis. Upregulated serine-glycine-one-carbon pathway in LKB1-mutant cells depletes extracellular serine, regulating T cell proliferation and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 are supported by appropriate citations. The metabolic competition between cancer cells and T cells for serine represents an important non-cell-autonomous mechanism of immune suppression. The mechanistic pathway is well-characterized, though the quantitative impact on T cell function in vivo requires further study.

results.result: KRAS/LKB1 co-mutations alter nitrogen metabolism and confer immunotherapy resistance: KRAS/LKB1 tumors show altered nitrogen metabolism. KRAS/LKB1-mutant cells depend on unorthodox pyrimidine biosynthesis using mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate through CPS1 upregulation. CPS1 confers resistance to arginine depletion, a strategy of pro-tumor macrophages to inhibit T cell responses. Primary PD-1 therapy resistance in KRAS-mutant patients is mainly associated with LKB1 alterations. Lkb1 ablation induces anti-PD-1/PD-L1 resistance in murine Kras-mutant models. KRAS/LKB1 mutations establish non-T cell inflamed TME with reduced CD3+/CD4+/CD8+ T cell infiltration and low PD-1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 are supported by citations to metabolic studies and clinical observations. The connection between LKB1 loss, altered metabolism, and immunotherapy resistance is well-documented. The mechanistic insights into CPS1-mediated arginine independence provide therapeutic opportunities. Clinical correlation strengthens translational relevance.

results.result: Immune system shapes tumor genomic landscape: Immunodeficient mice have increased tumor susceptibility and cancer cells from immunodeficient mice have higher immunogenicity compared to wild-type mice. Immunosuppressed transplant recipients developed secondary tumors after transplantation from undetected cancer of organ donors.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by appropriate citations. These observations provide evidence that the immune system exerts selective pressure on developing tumors. The transplant data provide compelling human evidence, though these are rare cases. This supports the concept of immunoediting.

results.result: Immune selection favors poorly presented oncogenic mutations: Mutations in known oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes have higher PHBR scores (less immune recognition probability) than random mutations. Positive correlation exists between PHBR score and mutation frequency in tumors. Oncogenic mutations can acquire high frequency not only from cell-autonomous fitness benefits but also from poor mutant peptide presentation, rendering mutations undetectable to immune cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by citation to the Marty et al. study introducing the PHBR score concept. This represents an important insight into how immune selection shapes the mutational landscape. However, this is based on computational predictions that would benefit from experimental validation of the proposed mechanism.

results.result: HLA LOH as immune escape mechanism: Tumors with clonal HLA LOH are associated with high neoantigen burden, APOBEC-mediated mutagenesis, and elevated PD-L1-positive immune cells compared to tumors without HLA LOH, suggesting HLA LOH is an immune escape mechanism. Cancer cell subclones with HLA LOH may be positively selected based on CD8+ T cell recognition evasion capability.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by citation to the McGranahan et al. study. HLA LOH as an immune escape mechanism is well-established. The association with high neoantigen burden suggests this occurs under immune selection pressure. The interpretation is logical though the specific dynamics of clonal selection require further study.

results.result: Single cytokine/chemokine targeting has limited efficacy: A comprehensive survey of clinical trials concluded that, with few exceptions, inhibiting or enhancing a single cytokine or chemokine pathway is unlikely to have sustained activity against advanced-stage cancer.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 is supported by citation to a comprehensive review. This represents an important clinical lesson from numerous failed trials. However, the CANTOS results (C60-C64) suggest IL-1β may be an exception, and the statement may be too broad given emerging combination therapy approaches.

results.result: Single-cell approaches reveal TME heterogeneity: At single-cell level, gene expression occurs stochastically with genes undergoing bursts and inactivity cycles. Combining whole-exome and transcriptomic data from >1000 ICI-treated patients with single-cell RNA-seq from neoantigen-reactive CD8+ TILs identified CCR5 and CXCL13 as T cell-intrinsic markers of ICI sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by appropriate citations. The stochastic gene expression concept is well-established. The identification of CCR5 and CXCL13 as ICI sensitivity markers represents an important application of single-cell approaches, though these markers require prospective validation.

results.result: TMB as FDA-approved biomarker: Meta-analysis showed high TMB (≥10 mut/Mb) significantly correlated with prolonged PFS in patients receiving PD-L1/PD-1 therapies. Pembrolizumab received FDA approval for adult and pediatric patients with unresectable or metastatic TMB-H ≥10 mut/Mb solid tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by appropriate citations. The FDA approval represents regulatory validation of TMB as a predictive biomarker. However, the authors appropriately note elsewhere that TMB has limitations including technical challenges, lack of standardized cutoffs, and imperfect predictive value.

results.result: Mutation-specific biomarkers for immunotherapy response: NSCLC patients with EGFR mutation showed unfavorable response to PD-L1/PD-1 inhibitors compared to wild-type EGFR, related to low TMB and immunosuppressive TME. HLA-I LOH is a negative predictor of overall survival in non-squamous NSCLC patients treated with ICIs. Combining TMB and HLA-I LOH improved survival prediction, suggesting better patient subcategorization for immunotherapy benefit.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by appropriate citations. The poor ICI response in EGFR-mutant patients is well-documented clinically. The combination of TMB and HLA-I LOH represents a rational approach to improve patient selection, though prospective validation is needed.

results.result: Spatial TME features predict survival: Lower density of anti-tumor M1-like macrophages and higher proximity of cancer cells to pro-tumor M2-like macrophages are associated with poor survival in NSCLC. Accumulation of Th9 and Th17 cells in lung tumors correlates with poor survival in lung cancer patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are supported by citations to the authors' own work using multiplex immunofluorescence. The spatial analysis approach is rigorous and the findings are consistent with TME biology. However, these are correlative observations that require validation in independent cohorts and mechanistic studies.

results.result: Metabolic vulnerabilities in LKB1-mutant tumors: LKB1 loss increases sensitivity to energetic stress triggered by metformin and phenformin. Enhanced dependence on CPS1-associated pyrimidine pool in KRAS/LKB1 mutated cells suggests higher sensitivity to DNA replication stress, which can lead to DNA damage and cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are supported by appropriate citations. These findings identify potential therapeutic vulnerabilities in LKB1-mutant tumors. The metabolic dependencies are well-characterized, though clinical translation of these vulnerabilities remains to be demonstrated.

results.result: Osimertinib efficacy and PD-L1 relationship: In ADAURA study, adjuvant osimertinib significantly improved disease-free survival in stage IB-IIIA EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Osimertinib can induce PD-L1 degradation and reduce PD-L1 mRNA in vitro, but clinical data on PD-L1 association with osimertinib is contradictory. Brown et al. showed osimertinib efficacy was unaffected by PD-L1 expression, while Hsu et al. reported strong PD-L1 expression associated with poorer prognosis in osimertinib-treated patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 present contradictory clinical findings regarding PD-L1's role in osimertinib response. While C116 is well-supported by the ADAURA trial, the conflicting results in C118-C119 highlight uncertainty in this area. The in vitro data (C117) may not reflect complex in vivo dynamics. Further studies are needed to resolve these discrepancies.

results.result: EGFR-TKI effects on TME are transient: EGFR-TKIs induce rapid, temporary increase of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, dendritic cells, and reduction of pro-tumor M2-macrophages in EGFR-driven mouse models. However, most anti-tumor effects gradually diminished with continued treatment while MDSCs consistently became more dominant during tumor development under treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by citation to mouse model studies. The transient nature of EGFR-TKI immune effects and MDSC accumulation provide important insights into resistance mechanisms. However, these are mouse model findings that require validation in human patients receiving EGFR-TKIs.

results.result: Macrophage reprogramming as therapeutic strategy: Chemotherapy-resistant KRAS patients have large populations of pro-tumor M2-macrophages supporting immunosuppressive TME phenotype. Re-programming M2-protumor macrophages through Wnt/β-catenin pathway modulation reduced primary and metastatic lung tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 are supported by appropriate citations. The concept of macrophage reprogramming is well-established. The Wnt/β-catenin modulation approach shows promise in preclinical models, though clinical translation and optimal therapeutic strategies remain to be determined.

results.result: Evolutionary model of TME-cancer cell co-evolution: In initial tumor growth, TME has tumor-suppressive phenotype with mainly anti-tumor immune cells (M1-like TAMs, CD8+ T cells). During progression, TME reaches steady state with anti-tumor and pro-tumor components in equilibrium. Through evolutionary selection, cancer cell clones with unique genomic landscape and higher fitness reshape TME to enhance pro-tumor components supporting growth and proliferation. Less fit clones are targeted by anti-tumor TME elements and depleted during progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 describe a conceptual model illustrated in Figure 1. This evolutionary framework is supported by the broader literature on tumor evolution and immunoediting. The model integrates multiple lines of evidence presented in the review, though it represents a simplified view of complex, dynamic processes.
